His fingers press into the bare skin of Mydei’s shoulder, and he can feel the battle-rough calluses on Phainon’s palm where his claymore’s hilt has rested day after day, swing after swing. Mydei thinks to swat Phainon’s hand away, but hesitates long enough that Phainon grows bolder, leaning even closer into Mydei’s space as if to demand his attention.

“Bold of you to make demands while you are a visitor in my chambers, hero.” Mydei parries the question bluntly, glancing at Phainon’s hand that lingers on his shoulder and weighing his options. He cannot decide if he'd rather Phainon stay or leave, and splashing him then kicking him out is a tempting variant.

Combat between two who cannot know death is a moment that stretches endlessly; an unending cycle of blood, battle, and rebirth. Every strike of Nikador’s golden lance reverberates through Mydei’s gauntlets, through his muscle and sinew, rattling his bones within his skin. The Titan fights the way he does: savagely, unyieldingly, without care of their own safety, just like an embodiment of Castrum Kremnos and their people. There is no finesse in the Lance of Fury’s strikes, none of the captivating technique that lets Phainon keep pace with Mydei when they spar - just the battle-hunger of a mad god caught in death throes for eternity.

It could have been minutes, hours, or days since Mydei sent Phainon and the travelers from beyond the sky away from the ruins of his home and the wrath of his god. The longer he lives, even off the battlefield, the more he marks the passage of time by death; Mydei himself has not changed since he grew into the prime of what should have been a mortal life. A war is marked by how dark the ground grows with blood, how much his armored boots sink into the mud of gore, how few remain while he continues to cleave a path forward. His life outside combat is marked by who remains at his side while he remains stuck in time.

This battle is marked in cycles of pain - a constant crescendo of combat, a cresting climax, and a blistering, agonizing, comet-tail contest of attrition. In these cycle-end skirmishes, where Mydei and Nikador all but tear themselves apart to pull the other down first, Mydei faintly envies his god’s madness.

Are Strife’s godly mind and body capable of feeling excruciating sensations analogous to bone shattering within muscle, tearing through the sinew and skin, and knowing that they must rise on broken limbs and raise their head and meet their end? Do they, too, feel instinctive, crawling dread claw up their throat when their body bends and breaks and they are thrown into that moment of twilight, even after a lifetime of death?

Kremnoans fight with nothing less than all they are imbued in every strike. They fight knowing that every strike might be their last, and if it is, they’ll accept nothing less than to go out in a blaze of valor. Mydei, too, fights this way - it’s ingrained in his mind and soul, hammered into his marrow - but no strike will ever be his last. And yet, he never pulls his punches.

Nikador’s lance clangs against the metal of Mydei’s gauntlets over and over, metal shrieking against metal, weapons cutting through the otherwise oppressive silence of Castrum Kremnos. The sound soothes Mydei, in a way - otherwise, it is only his shouts of exertion and pain that echo through the ruins of his home.

“Mydei!”

Phainon’s shout of his name injects life into the stagnant loop of combat. There is no hesitation as Mydei instinctively twists his body to the left, catching Nikador’s lance with one gauntlet and making room for Phainon’s claymore to swing up from the right, slamming into the edge of the lance beside him. No words are needed as they parry the strike in sync, standing shoulder to shoulder. This time, Nikador’s lance does not bear down so heavily that Mydei thinks it might push him into the floor. Phainon is warm at his side.

“You’re here,” Mydei says in acknowledgement, jumping back in step with Phainon as Nikador draws back their lance once more. He intends to glance at Phainon and then return his attention to the fight, but ends up looking a moment too long when he sees Phainon unabashedly scanning him up and down for injury.

“Sorry I’m late,” Phainon says, eyes flitting back to Mydei’s. There is nothing of note for Phainon to see - some scrapes and bruises from this round, but Mydei’s last revival was not very long ago.

Mydei just scoffs, a nonverbal rebuttal to the apology. He is used to fighting alone, but he won’t tell Phainon his presence isn’t desired. “Sword up, hero,” Mydei says instead, sinking back into a combat-ready stance. He gives Phainon precisely the amount of space he needs to swing his claymore, but stands close enough to cover his back. He watches the glint of Nikador’s lance as they raise it high, the tip aimed downwards. “Are you ready?”

Phainon, too, readies himself for battle. His claymore is held to his right, opposite Mydei, and he gives Mydei a grin, disarming in its openness. “Always,” Phainon says, and there is no fear or hesitation in his tone or expression. He is honest, confident, and so fearless that he does not seem out of place in Castrum Kremnos. He is so bright that Mydei has to look away.

“Focus,” Mydei chides, looking back at Nikador. Phainon laughs, then, and Mydei does not know if he’s scolding Phainon or himself.

-—-

Mydei had been asked once, many years ago, what dreams lie at the bottom of his heart. When his answer was metaphorical, he’d been asked instead, “A vanguard, an aegis, or a marksman?”

[Little crown prince Mydeimos had answered with none of them. No lance or shield or bow was forged for him - no weapon or armor could grant him the dreams of adventure and light that fluttered in the depths of his heart. But when he was forced to choose, he found his answer. Not with a lance or bow or shield, but with his whole body.]

The answer is obvious from a single glance - no armor adorns Mydei’s chest, nor is he built for anything but offense. He’s a singular arrow shot into the ranks of his enemies to tear them down one by one, not the archer at the bow nor the aegis to stand as shield between blade and bone.

Mydei fights with calculated abandon, willing to suffer for every strike so long as no injury goes unrepaid. He leaps forward to trade blows with Nikador when Phainon catches the lance on his claymore, uncaring of how far past the limits of his body he pushes. He pivots on his heel to cover Phainon’s back when he swings his claymore wide, stopping Nikador’s strikes with his bare body, trusting Phainon to follow up and keep the rhythm of the fight.

Mydei is the weapon himself. He is the vanguard, the aegis, the marksman - but he is alone. He stands at the frontline, he never allows himself to fall without getting up again, he launches himself into enemy ranks. It has always been this way, and in Mydei’s most pessimistic moments he thinks it may always remain like this.

And yet, as Nikador’s lance reaches its apex and cleaves downwards after a sweeping blow that knocked Mydei to the ground, he has staggered to his feet and planted himself in front of Phainon.

At once, the lance is stained with another layer of molten gold blood and Phainon’s shout is all but drowned out by the sickening squelch and snap of Nikador’s weapon passing clean through Mydei’s chest - breaking the breastbone and puncturing his insides - and despite all of Mydei’s efforts, just barely stops short of piercing Phainon behind him.

It unsheathes itself from Mydei with a wet sound, followed by the splatter of shimmering blood that cascades from the wound. The pain is so intense it eclipses into icy shock, and only when Mydei coughs, another waterfall of liquid gold falling from his lips, does the searing burn of it begin to ignite through his body. It makes his muscles seize and shudder, and then the ground is coming up to meet him.

Instead of Mydei’s armored knees crashing to the hard stone beneath him, a firm arm winds around his waist and holds him up with enough care to jolt him back to the battlefield. When he turns his head, ignoring the blistering sensation of his body knitting itself together again, he is met with Phainon’s wide blue eyes, racing thoughts so obviously at the tip of his tongue as his lips part hesitantly, moonlight hair sticking to his face with sweat and grime.

“Eyes forward,” Mydei chides again, and his voice comes out like a death rattle as his half-formed lungs struggle to give him air. His chest constricts, surely from the effort. “Not on me.”

Phainon’s eyes flicker from Mydei’s face to the gold dripping from his chin to his chest, where his muscles and flesh are growing back together. There’s a distant look on Phainon’s face, like he gets sometimes when he talks about himself without saying very much at all - but Mydei knows the feeling that pulls at the edge of his lips. What is it, if not loneliness?

“Phainon,” Mydei says, when the moment stretches on too long and Phainon’s gaze becomes too heavy for Mydei to want to unpack. His voice is a wet rasp. Mydei doesn't often call Phainon by name - for he has his own suspicions to Phainon’s secrets, not that they are anything for him to ask about - but the word is enough for Phainon to snap out of it.

Phainon’s fingers curl tighter around his waist briefly, as if loath to let go, before he lets out a little exhale. “I know,” Phainon says, but his eyes keep drifting downwards towards the mortal wound healing all on its own. “But -“

Mydei growls in exertion as he leans over to grasp Phainon’s other hand, hanging at his side and still holding his claymore, and forces him to swing it up. The blade clangs against Nikador’s lance, and Phainon instantly refocuses and helps Mydei repel the strike.

“Not the time,” Mydei says, breathing still ragged. He’ll need another few moments to be able to parry a strike like that on his own.

The sensation of Phainon’s arm around him, against his back, hand on his waist, is so distracting that he only belatedly realizes that he’s whole again.

For the first time in a long while, Mydei’s thoughts are blessedly quiet - bone deep exhaustion surely plays a part, but there’s a deeper sense of peace knowing that Nikador’s undying body no longer haunts Castrum Kremnos. Faintly, Mydei wonders what it would take to put him to rest, too.
